data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The search for evidence distinguishing genuine reliability from mere compliance within a single evaluation is ill-posed if the evaluation is a standard black-box test: from the outside, a system that genuinely understands the checklist and a system that blindly executes it are observationally equivalent on all cases where the checklist is correct. The only within-evaluation evidence is a compliance audit, which is not a judgment-quality measure.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the evaluation is allowed to be a white-box or process-tracing evaluation, then internal evidence is available and the claim is false.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If one accepts 'step-by-step intermediate answers' as part of the evaluation output, then the black-box assumption is violated and the test is possible.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the checklist has a known failure mode that is always triggered by a specific input pattern, that pattern serves as an effective within-evaluation probe even in a black-box setting.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The problem asks for evidence within a single evaluation, but an evaluation typically measures only input-output behavior. If the panel and the expert are treated as black boxes, their internal processes (genuine understanding vs rote compliance) are hidden. A compliance audit (did they tick the boxes?) is process evidence but does not, by itself, show the reliability gain is due to understanding rather than compliance. To get the evidence, one must open the box, which changes the nature of the evaluation from a judgment evaluation to a process evaluation. So the request for evidence within a single (black-box) evaluation may be impossible to satisfy.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
